title: Buffered I/O — where the bytes are waiting

opening.title: One character operation need not mean one system call
keyPoints: A library can retain bytes in user memory
Larger transfers share fixed call overhead
The same buffering delays visibility
opening.narration: Writing a character through a library does not necessarily enter the kernel immediately. A user-space buffer can collect many characters and send them together. This reduces repeated transition and setup costs, but it also means the application's successful operation may precede the underlying transfer. Those are two sides of the same mechanism. Begin with the question of who currently holds the bytes. Are they still in the application buffer, accepted by the kernel, or covered by the required persistence operation? Naming that boundary prevents a performance explanation from becoming an incorrect promise that every formatted line is already safely stored.
actions: Track one byte through the application buffer and underlying write path.

question.prompt: Why can buffering both improve efficiency and delay visible output?
question.answer: Several operations share a later transfer, so bytes may remain in user memory before that transfer occurs.

opening.title: Count elements when the interface counts elements
keyPoints: fwrite returns complete elements
Element size one makes counts equal bytes
A zero byte is still valid block data
opening.narration: The program writes three elements of two bytes each to an automatically removed temporary file. fwrite returns three, not six, because its result counts complete elements. After an explicit positioning transition, fread requests six elements of size one and returns six. The zero byte at index two remains zero, so it does not terminate this block operation. The output makes the units visible: written-elements three, read-bytes six, and embedded-zero zero. Every count is checked before reporting success, and fclose is checked too. This is a correctness demonstration of standard I/O, not a measurement of how many kernel calls the library chose or proof of durable storage.
actions: Predict counts and zero-byte behavior before Run.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch35.json → SP35.008 · 35.3 Standard I/O

question.prompt: Why do the write and read counts differ although the same six bytes move?
question.answer: The write element size is two, while the read element size is one. Counts are in elements.

opening.title: The library position can be ahead of the application
keyPoints: Read-ahead fetches a block
The application may consume only its first byte
Raw descriptor reads use the underlying offset
opening.narration: Suppose a library reads ABCD from the underlying file to satisfy an application request for A. The underlying file position is now four, while B, C, and D wait in the library buffer. A later buffered read can return B without another system call. A raw descriptor read instead begins at the underlying position and may return E. Nothing disappeared from storage; the program mixed two layers whose positions differ. This explains why FILE pointers and integer descriptors are not interchangeable abstractions. Choose one for a workflow unless there is a deliberate synchronization plan that accounts for read-ahead, pending writes, and position changes.
actions: Mark separate application-consumption and descriptor positions.

question.prompt: Where are B, C, and D after the application receives only A?
question.answer: They can already be in the library’s read buffer, even though the underlying offset advanced past them.

opening.title: Model the apparent skipped bytes safely
keyPoints: The model explicitly fetches four bytes
Buffered next is B
Raw next is E because the underlying offset is four
opening.narration: This portable model intentionally uses strings so we can show both positions without performing an improperly coordinated mix of real I/O. Fetching the first four bytes advances kernel_position to four. The application consumes A from the local buffer, leaving its index at one. Reading through that buffer next yields B, while a modeled raw read at the underlying position yields E. The three printed characters therefore explain the apparent gap exactly. The model does not claim that every real library reads four bytes; that size is chosen to make the mechanism visible. A real implementation's read-ahead amount is an implementation detail.
actions: Predict all three characters before Run.
opening.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch35.json → SP35.010 · 35.4 FILE*

question.prompt: Does the model prove that real stdio always reads four bytes ahead?
question.answer: No. Four is a teaching parameter; the separation between buffered consumption and underlying position is the mechanism.

code.model: Explicit read-ahead and offset model; no FILE/descriptor mixing is executed.

mechanism.title: FILE* is a library-managed object, not an fd
keyPoints: The stream tracks buffers and error state
fileno exposes an associated descriptor on POSIX
Owning both views does not make them independent
mechanism.narration: FILE* is a pointer to a library-managed stream with more state than a descriptor number. It may retain unread input, unwritten output, and an error or end-of-file indicator. On POSIX, fileno can reveal its underlying descriptor, but that does not duplicate the stream's buffer or ownership. Closing the raw descriptor behind the stream can leave later stream operations trying to use a released number. Conversely, closing the stream normally releases its associated resource, so another blind close risks misuse. Document whether helpers borrow the stream or own it, and prefer one abstraction for the normal path. Pointer and integer syntax alone do not settle ownership.
actions: Ask who closes the resource after a helper borrows FILE*.

question.prompt: Does fileno create a separate stream with an independent buffer?
question.answer: No. It exposes the associated descriptor; the original FILE object still owns its library state.

mechanism.title: A supplied buffer must outlive its stream use
keyPoints: setvbuf can borrow caller-provided storage
Configure buffering before other operations as required
Do not return with the stream still borrowing a local array
mechanism.narration: If a stream is configured to use an array supplied by the application, that array becomes part of the stream's lifetime contract. A local array inside a setup helper disappears when the helper returns, but the stream may keep using its address. That creates a dangling buffer even though the FILE pointer itself remains valid. Use storage whose lifetime covers the required stream use and configure it at the correct stage before other operations. A simple library-managed buffer is often safer unless a concrete need justifies custom storage. This is the same ownership reasoning used for borrowed views: the borrower cannot outlive the bytes it accesses.
actions: Trace the array lifetime separately from the FILE object lifetime.

question.prompt: Why is a local array in a returning setup helper a bad long-lived stream buffer?
question.answer: Its lifetime ends while the stream can still retain and use its address.

mechanism.title: Flush, close, and durable commit are different promises
keyPoints: fflush transfers pending library output
fclose may fail during final output work
Kernel acceptance is not the same as durable storage
mechanism.narration: A successful formatting call may only have filled a user-space buffer. fflush asks the library to send pending output through its underlying path and can report failure. fclose can encounter failure while completing the same kind of pending work, so ignoring its result can hide lost output. Neither operation alone means the storage device has met a durable-update contract. The kernel may still hold data in its own cache. A persistence requirement needs the documented synchronization and filesystem steps appropriate to the application. Keep those promises separate in names and tests: a buffered-I/O correctness check is not a power-loss recovery test.
actions: Ask learners to name the next layer after the library buffer.

question.prompt: What does successful fflush establish that a formatting call alone may not?
question.answer: Pending library output has been passed through the stream’s underlying output path under its contract; it still does not prove durable storage.

mechanism.title: Three caches can affect one file operation
keyPoints: User-space buffering belongs to the library
The kernel page cache retains file data
CPU caches accelerate accesses to memory
mechanism.narration: A repeated file test may become faster because the kernel already has the file's pages, because the library already buffered input, or because the relevant memory is hot in CPU caches. Those mechanisms are distinct even when they all reduce waiting. Calling every result disk speed hides what was actually exercised. A warm-cache copy might mainly measure memory copies and kernel paths rather than storage media. State the destination and buffering mode, use controlled fixtures, and avoid disruptive system-wide cache manipulation in an ordinary lab. The useful conclusion is tied to the tested conditions, so preserve those conditions with the reported measurements.
actions: Identify which layer each proposed timing experiment actually exercises.

question.prompt: Why is a warm repeated read not automatically a storage-device benchmark?
question.answer: The data may be served from memory caches without the same device work as an uncached read.

closing.title: A buffer-size experiment needs equal useful work
keyPoints: Hold total bytes and destination fixed
Keep error handling equivalent
Measure response delay as well as throughput when relevant
closing.narration: Comparing one-byte writes to block writes only explains call overhead if other conditions stay comparable. Writing to a terminal can include rendering and terminal processing, while writing to a temporary file has different costs. Both versions must transfer the same bytes and check completion. A larger buffer may improve total throughput while delaying the first visible result or cancellation response. Those are legitimate costs rather than noise to hide. Start from a correctness test that compares exact output, then measure controlled variants. A maintenance change should preserve required flush boundaries instead of trading them away for an attractive aggregate timing number.
actions: Choose a shared endpoint and identical payload for both variants.

question.prompt: What could confound a comparison where one version writes to a terminal and another to a file?
question.answer: Endpoint behavior and rendering work differ, so the result does not isolate buffering or system-call overhead.

closing.title: Recall where the bytes are waiting
keyPoints: Library buffering changes call frequency
Read-ahead separates two positions
Completion must be checked at the required boundary
closing.narration: The most useful question in a buffered-I/O bug is where the bytes are now. They may be waiting in a library output buffer, already fetched into its input buffer, accepted into kernel-managed state, or beyond the required persistence boundary. The element-count demo showed why units matter; the read-ahead model showed why mixing layers can skip over bytes from the application's viewpoint. Keep ownership and lifetime visible for the stream and any supplied buffer. Then choose the smallest interface that meets the job. A clear buffered workflow with explicit transitions is easier to verify than scattered raw operations around an otherwise buffered program.
actions: Explain one delayed-output symptom using the buffer’s current owner.
closing.sourceRef: content/systems-programming/ch35.json → SP35.022 · Worked example — Flush boundaries

question.prompt: What should you inspect when a prompt never appears before input waits?
question.answer: The output buffer and its required flush policy, while checking output errors rather than assuming the formatting call reached the user.
